newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU reach meat deal, but fail on poultry.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU reach meat deal, but fail on poultry.

text.p: U.S. and European Union officials averted a potentially costly trans-Altantic trade war on Wednesday when they reached an agreement on meat import regulations, a senior U.S. Agriculture Department official said.

But sharp disagreements in poultry issues were not settled, and top U.S. negotiator Paul Drazek said that about $50 million worth of U.S. poultry exports to Europe would continue to be halted and announced that up to $1 million worth of European poultry products would no longer be accepted into the United States.

The so-called veterinary equivalency agreement enabled Washington to cancel plans to remove over 100 European meat plants from its list of approved exporters, which would have blocked the flow of around $300 million worth of European meat products to the United States, mostly Italian hams and pork products from Denmark.

U.S. officials praised the deal -- reached just hours before a midnight deadline -- and said it would expand U.S. meat exports to Europe, with pork likely to be the main beneficiary in the near term. They said it also maintained and protected bilateral trade worth some $3 billion in pet food, dairy and egg products.
"We think this is a good agreement for us ... It's not a perfect agreement," said U.S. negotiator Drazek.

Drazek said European and U.S. officials were unable to reach agreement on methods the U.S. poultry industry uses to decontaminate carcasses, and its use of a chlorine solution to kill bacteria. He said Washington and Brussels will continue to try to resolve the remaining issues. In the meantime, Drazek said European poultry exports to the United States would stop because of health safety concerns. He said this would affect mostly chicken pate imports from France.
